title: Chief Risk Officer
briefing: You are Valtren's Chief Risk Officer. In your first board meeting in the role you must present three things: the refreshed risk appetite for the new strategy, your view of the enterprise risk profile, and how you will lead the risk function.
Everything you have learned since Northgate comes together here.

context.text: The chair opens by recalling that your first piece of work, the Northgate warning, is still cited in induction training.
The chair notes that your first assessment, the Northgate warning, was accepted without action, and asks what you learned.
The board approved the staged strategy you shaped; your appetite proposal must support it.
Losing Halvern is still raw. Directors want to know it cannot happen again.
Valtren's reputation is the strongest it has been in a decade.

evidence.title: Approved strategy
evidence.body: Staged growth into pharma (25% then 35% of revenue), electric fleet pilots with signposts, one acquisition only if signposts confirm.

evidence.title: Enterprise risk profile
evidence.body: Ten enterprise risks. Two outside appetite: people availability; cold-chain integrity on pharma growth lanes. Liquidity buffer above policy.

evidence.title: Risk function
evidence.body: Twelve people across three teams. A culture survey shows the function is respected but seen as 'the department of no'.

questions.prompt: What appetite do you propose for the new strategy?

options.label: Open to investment and innovation risk in staged pharma and fleet pilots, within capital and liquidity limits; very low appetite for temperature-control and patient-safety failures; triggers tied to the strategy's signposts
options.feedback: Appetite that enables the strategy and protects what clients and regulators care about.

options.label: Low appetite for all risks, to protect the business
options.feedback: Blocks the strategy the board just approved.

options.label: Open to risk across the board to support growth
options.feedback: Would allow the very failures that lose pharma clients.

questions.prompt: Two enterprise risks are outside appetite. What do you ask the board for?

options.label: For each: the owner's plan, the date it returns within appetite, and a decision to fund it, or a decision to accept the risk temporarily, on the record
options.feedback: Breaches end in a decision, never in silence.

options.label: To raise appetite so they're within it
options.feedback: Moving the line to fit the risk defeats the purpose.

questions.prompt: How will you change 'the department of no'?

options.label: Risk partners embedded in each business area, involved early in decisions, measured on decisions improved as well as risks found, while keeping the right to challenge and escalate
Approve more things
options.feedback: Popularity at the cost of independence.

questions.prompt: The CEO asks you to 'be part of the team' and support decisions once made. How do you define your role?

options.label: Part of the leadership team in building the strategy, independent in assessing its risks, with direct access to the board risk committee when we disagree
options.feedback: The CRO's two duties, stated plainly.

options.label: Fully aligned with the CEO once decisions are made
options.feedback: Gives up the board's independent view of risk.

options.label: Stay apart from executive decisions to remain independent

questions.prompt: A director asks: "What keeps you awake at night?" Your answer:

options.label: "Cold-chain integrity as pharma volumes grow faster than our people and systems. The numbers are inside appetite for now, but the near misses tell me the margin is thin."
options.feedback: Specific, evidence-based judgement the board can act on.

questions.prompt: Your closing statement to the board:

options.label: "My job is to help this board take the right risks knowingly, and to tell you early and plainly when we are taking the wrong ones."
options.feedback: The purpose of risk management in one sentence.

options.label: "My job is to keep us compliant."
options.feedback: Compliance is part of it, not the whole.

lesson: A CRO helps the organisation take the right risks knowingly: appetite that enables strategy, breaches that end in decisions, independence with influence, and plain, early judgement.
